subject: ENT
q: Which paranasal sinus is the most common site of acute and chronic sinusitis?
why: Correct — high ostium and dental proximity make it the commonest site
Frontal sinusitis is less common and follows nasofrontal duct obstruction
Sphenoid sinusitis is rarest but most dangerous given proximity to the cavernous sinus/pituitary
Ethmoid sinusitis is common in young children but maxillary disease is overall commonest
exp: The maxillary sinus is the most common site of sinusitis because its ostium lies high on the medial wall well above the sinus floor, giving poor dependent drainage; it is also the largest sinus and closely related to premolar/molar roots, making dental infection an important cause of unilateral disease.

subject: ENT
q: A 25-year-old man has chronic foul postnasal discharge and dull occipital headache; nasopharyngoscopy shows a midline cystic swelling on the posterior nasopharyngeal wall. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Angiofibroma causes recurrent epistaxis with a vascular mass, not a midline cyst
Correct — notochordal remnant cyst causing chronic discharge and occipital headache
Adenoid cystic carcinoma is a salivary-type malignancy, not a benign cyst
Rathke's pouch forms the anterior pituitary, not a nasopharyngeal cyst
exp: Tornwaldt's cyst is a benign midline nasopharyngeal cyst arising from a persistent notochordal remnant/pharyngeal bursa, presenting with chronic foul postnasal discharge, halitosis and occipital headache, distinguishing it from angiofibroma.

subject: ENT
q: A 55-year-old diabetic man has severe ear pain, vesicles over the pinna and external canal, ipsilateral facial weakness, and sensorineural hearing loss. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Bell's palsy has no vesicles or hearing loss
AOM causes otalgia with a bulging drum, not vesicles or facial palsy
Correct — vesicles plus facial palsy and SNHL indicate VZV reactivation
Malignant otitis externa shows granulation tissue in diabetics, not a vesicular eruption
exp: Ramsay Hunt syndrome is reactivation of latent VZV in the geniculate ganglion, giving the triad of severe otalgia, vesicles on the pinna/canal, and ipsilateral facial palsy, often with SNHL and vertigo; it has a worse facial recovery prognosis than Bell's palsy.

subject: ENT
q: A 4-year-old unimmunized child has sudden high fever, drooling, muffled voice, and sits leaning forward with the neck extended. What is the most appropriate immediate step?
opts: Lateral neck X-ray before any intervention
Direct visualization with a tongue depressor at the bedside
Nebulized racemic epinephrine and discharge if improved
Secure the airway under controlled conditions in the OT with a senior anaesthetist/ENT surgeon present
why: Imaging delays definitive management and can precipitate obstruction
Bedside instrumentation can trigger fatal laryngospasm
Epinephrine nebulization is croup management, not epiglottitis
Correct — controlled OT airway securing is the safest approach
exp: Acute epiglottitis can obstruct completely if the throat is instrumented or the child is agitated; the cardinal rule is to avoid examining the throat and instead secure the airway electively in the OT with anaesthesia and ENT back-up for emergency tracheostomy.

subject: ENT
q: A 19-year-old man, one week after a sore throat, develops high fever, tender neck swelling along the sternocleidomastoid, and bilateral cavitary lung lesions on chest X-ray. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — post-anginal IJV thrombophlebitis with septic pulmonary emboli
Peritonsillar abscess causes trismus and uvular deviation, not lung lesions
Retropharyngeal abscess causes neck stiffness/stridor in children, not septic emboli
Ludwig's angina is submandibular cellulitis threatening the airway, without lung involvement
exp: Lemierre syndrome is septic thrombophlebitis of the internal jugular vein, classically following oropharyngeal infection with Fusobacterium necrophorum, presenting with tender neck swelling and septic pulmonary emboli — an important diagnosis in a young adult with post-anginal sepsis and cavitary lung lesions.

subject: ENT
q: A 20-year-old competitive swimmer has severe ear pain and itching with scanty discharge; pulling the pinna and pressing the tragus sharply worsens the pain, and hearing is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Furunculosis of the external auditory canal
why: Furunculosis is a localized tender pustule, not diffuse canal inflammation
Correct — diffuse post-water-exposure canal inflammation with tragal tenderness
Otitis media does not cause tragal tenderness since the canal is uninvolved
Malignant OE occurs in diabetics with granulation tissue and cranial nerve palsies, not a healthy young swimmer
exp: Acute diffuse otitis externa is cellulitis/dermatitis of the canal skin after water exposure macerates the skin and disrupts the acidic cerumen barrier; the hallmark is pain reproduced by tragal pressure or pinna traction.

subject: ENT
q: Which cranial nerve carries the afferent (sensory) limb of the gag reflex from the posterior pharyngeal wall?
why: Trigeminal supplies facial/anterior tongue sensation, not the pharyngeal wall
Facial nerve carries taste from the anterior 2/3 tongue and supplies facial muscles, not pharyngeal sensation
Correct — glossopharyngeal is the afferent limb
Vagus is the efferent, not afferent, limb
exp: The gag reflex afferent limb runs via the glossopharyngeal nerve; the efferent (motor) limb runs via the vagus.

subject: ENT
q: A child with chronic ear discharge develops severe retro-orbital pain and a lateral (VI nerve) squint on the same side. Which complication of otitis media does this triad suggest?
why: Bezold's abscess is pus tracking into the sternocleidomastoid, presenting as upper-neck swelling, not orbital pain/squint
Sinus thrombophlebitis classically causes spiking picket-fence fever, not this cranial-nerve triad
Correct — Gradenigo syndrome is otorrhoea plus retro-orbital pain (CN V) plus lateral rectus palsy (CN VI) from petrous apex infection along Dorello's canal
Labyrinthitis causes vertigo and sensorineural hearing loss, not a VI nerve palsy
exp: Gradenigo syndrome — otorrhoea, retro-orbital/facial pain, and an abducens (CN VI) palsy — results from petrous apicitis tracking infection along Dorello's canal, where CN VI runs close to the petrous apex.

subject: ENT
q: Which paired paranasal sinus is present and pneumatized at birth, making ethmoiditis/orbital cellulitis a recognized entity in infancy?
why: Correct — ethmoid (and maxillary) sinuses are present and pneumatized at birth
Frontal sinus is rudimentary/absent at birth, pneumatizing around age 6-8
Sphenoid pneumatizes later in childhood
Incorrect — ethmoid (and maxillary) sinuses are present at birth
exp: The ethmoid and maxillary sinuses are present and pneumatized at birth; the frontal sinus starts pneumatizing around age 6-8 and the sphenoid later, explaining why ethmoiditis (not frontal sinusitis) occurs in infancy.

subject: ENT
q: Which is the sole abductor muscle of the vocal cords, whose bilateral paralysis (as can occur after thyroidectomy) causes airway obstruction requiring emergency tracheostomy?
why: Lateral cricoarytenoid is an adductor
Correct — posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor
Thyroarytenoid relaxes/adducts the cords
Cricothyroid tenses the cords (pitch), supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, not an abductor
exp: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor of the vocal cords; bilateral paralysis leaves the cords paramedian, causing airway obstruction and stridor.

subject: ENT
q: On tympanometry, a flat (Type B) curve with normal ear canal volume is most consistent with which condition?
opts: Eustachian tube dysfunction with a retracted TM (Type C)
why: Otosclerosis typically shows a Type As (shallow peak, reduced compliance) curve, not flat
Ossicular discontinuity classically shows Type Ad (deep, high-compliance peak)
Correct — a flat Type B tympanogram means the TM is essentially immobile, classically from middle-ear fluid
Type C shows a negative-pressure peak, not a flat curve
exp: A flat Type B tympanogram indicates a non-mobile tympanic membrane, classically from middle-ear effusion; a normal canal volume excludes a perforation.

subject: ENT
q: In a young adult with progressive conductive hearing loss and a normal-looking tympanic membrane, otoscopy reveals a flamingo-pink hue through the drum overlying the promontory (Schwartze's sign). This is characteristic of:
why: CSOM shows a perforation and discharge, not an intact drum with a vascular blush.
Glomus tympanicum shows a distinct pulsatile reddish mass (positive Brown's sign) with pulsatile tinnitus, not a diffuse blush.
Cholesteatoma shows an attic or marginal perforation with keratin debris, not a pink blush through an intact drum.
Correct — Schwartze's sign reflects increased vascularity of active otospongiotic bone in otosclerosis.
exp: Schwartze's sign (a flamingo-pink blush through an intact tympanic membrane over the promontory) reflects increased vascularity of active otospongiotic bone in otosclerosis, supporting the diagnosis along with a Carhart's notch on audiometry and family history.

subject: ENT
q: A child with untreated sinusitis develops a soft, fluctuant, tender forehead swelling with fever; imaging confirms frontal bone osteomyelitis with a subperiosteal abscess (Pott's puffy tumor). This most commonly arises from infection of which sinus?
why: Correct — Pott's puffy tumor is a complication of frontal sinusitis, with infection spreading via valveless diploic veins to the frontal bone.
Maxillary sinusitis more often causes orbital cellulitis or dental infection spread, not a forehead swelling.
Sphenoid sinusitis is notorious for cavernous sinus thrombosis and cranial nerve palsies, not a puffy tumor.
Ethmoid sinusitis in children classically causes orbital/periorbital cellulitis, not frontal bone osteomyelitis.
exp: Pott's puffy tumor complicates frontal sinusitis, with infection spreading via valveless diploic veins to cause frontal bone osteomyelitis and a subperiosteal forehead abscess; it carries a risk of intracranial extension and needs urgent imaging, antibiotics, and surgical drainage.

subject: ENT
q: A 34-year-old woman reports chronic dull throat and neck pain radiating to the ear, worse on turning her head, five years after tonsillectomy; palpation of the tonsillar fossa reproduces the pain.
why: TMJ pain is pre-auricular and chewing-related, no tonsillar fossa tenderness
Correct: post-tonsillectomy fibrosis around an elongated styloid reproduces pain on fossa palpation and head rotation
Recurrent abscess causes acute febrile episodes, not chronic dull pain
Glossopharyngeal neuralgia is brief lancinating pain triggered by swallowing, not by fossa palpation
exp: Eagle syndrome follows post-tonsillectomy fibrosis around an elongated styloid process or calcified stylohyoid ligament; pain is reproduced by tonsillar fossa palpation and worsens with head rotation, diagnosed on CT with 3D reconstruction and treated with styloidectomy.

subject: ENT
q: A 3-year-old child presents with progressive hoarseness of voice for six months and intermittent stridor, born to a mother with genital warts during pregnancy.
why: Vocal nodules follow voice abuse, not linked to maternal HPV, no stridor
Subglottic hemangioma presents earlier, under 6 months, with biphasic stridor worsening on crying
Correct: juvenile RRP follows vertical HPV 6/11 transmission during vaginal delivery, causing progressive hoarseness and stridor
Laryngeal web is congenital, present from birth with weak cry, not progressive over months
exp: Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis follows vertical transmission of HPV 6/11 from maternal genital warts at delivery, presenting with progressive hoarseness and stridor; treated with microdebrider excision, but recurrence is common and there is no cure.

subject: ENT
q: A 65-year-old hypertensive man has profuse bilateral nasal bleeding with blood draining posteriorly into the throat despite anterior nasal packing.
opts: Sphenopalatine artery bleed requiring posterior packing/endoscopic ligation
Little's area bleed from Kiesselbach's plexus
why: Correct: posterior epistaxis in elderly hypertensives typically arises from the sphenopalatine artery supplying Woodruff's plexus
Little's area bleeds are anterior and usually controlled with anterior packing/cautery, more common in the young
Anterior ethmoidal bleeds are high septal/roof bleeds, usually traumatic
Septal perforation is a complication of repeated cautery/trauma, not a bleeding source itself
exp: Posterior epistaxis in elderly hypertensive patients typically arises from the sphenopalatine artery, a maxillary artery branch supplying Woodruff's plexus; it fails anterior packing and needs posterior packing or endoscopic sphenopalatine artery cautery or ligation.

subject: ENT
q: A 45-year-old woman with long-standing iron deficiency anaemia complains of progressive difficulty swallowing solids, glossitis, and brittle spoon-shaped nails; barium swallow shows a thin web at the postcricoid region.
why: Achalasia shows bird-beak lower esophageal narrowing, dysphagia to both liquids and solids, not linked to iron deficiency
Carcinoma shows an irregular destructive stricture, usually with weight loss, not this classic triad
Zenker's diverticulum arises through Killian's dehiscence causing regurgitation and halitosis, seen as an outpouching not a web
Correct: Plummer-Vinson syndrome combines iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, postcricoid web, and glossitis/koilonychia
exp: Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome combines iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, a postcricoid esophageal web, and glossitis/koilonychia; it is premalignant for postcricoid squamous cell carcinoma and is treated with iron replacement and web dilatation.

subject: ENT
q: A 6-year-old unimmunized child presents with fever, sore throat, and a grayish-white membrane over the tonsils and pharynx that bleeds on attempted removal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Streptococcal exudate wipes off easily without bleeding
Correct — a bleeding pseudomembrane extending beyond the tonsillar pillars is the discriminating sign of diphtheria
Mono causes exudative tonsillitis with lymphadenopathy/splenomegaly but not a bleeding membrane
Peritonsillar abscess shows trismus and uvular deviation, no membrane
exp: An adherent, bleeding pseudomembrane extending beyond the tonsils onto the pharynx/palate is classic for diphtheria (Corynebacterium diphtheriae); the exotoxin risks myocarditis and demyelinating neuropathy, and it remains vaccine-preventable via DPT.

subject: ENT
q: A 68-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents with severe ear pain, foul discharge, and granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the external auditory canal. Which organism is most likely responsible?
why: S. aureus causes simple furunculosis of the canal, not this necrotizing pattern
Aspergillus causes otomycosis with fungal debris, not granulation tissue at this site
S. pneumoniae is a middle ear/sinus pathogen, not a cause of otitis externa
Correct — Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic organism in diabetic malignant otitis externa
exp: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa occurs in elderly diabetics/immunocompromised patients and is caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa; granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction is pathognomonic, and untreated disease progresses to skull base osteomyelitis with cranial nerve palsies (especially CN VII).

subject: ENT
q: A young adult presents with a saddle-nose deformity, chronic sinusitis, and hemoptysis; serum testing shows c-ANCA (anti-PR3) positivity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct — GPA presents with the upper/lower respiratory tract plus renal triad and is c-ANCA/PR3 positive
Rhinoscleroma is caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis with Mikulicz cells on biopsy, not ANCA-positive
Relapsing polychondritis affects cartilage (ear + nose) but is not c-ANCA associated
NK/T-cell lymphoma is a midline destructive EBV-associated lesion diagnosed on biopsy, not serology
exp: GPA is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis with the classic triad of upper respiratory (saddle nose, chronic sinusitis), lower respiratory (hemoptysis), and renal (glomerulonephritis) involvement; c-ANCA with anti-PR3 specificity is highly sensitive and specific, and treatment is immunosuppression.

subject: ENT
q: A 6-week-old infant has inspiratory stridor that worsens with feeding and supine positioning but improves when prone, without cyanosis or feeding difficulty. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Subglottic hemangioma causes biphasic stridor that progressively worsens over weeks, often with cutaneous hemangiomas
Vocal cord palsy causes a weak/breathy cry and biphasic stridor, usually from birth trauma or a CNS cause
Correct — positional stridor worse supine/feeding, better prone, is classic laryngomalacia
Croup is acute-onset with fever and a barking cough, not a chronic positional pattern
exp: Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of stridor in infancy, due to a floppy omega-shaped epiglottis and short aryepiglottic folds that prolapse into the airway on inspiration; it is positional, diagnosed by flexible laryngoscopy, and typically self-resolves by 12-18 months.

subject: ENT
q: A 45-year-old presents with progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and an absent corneal reflex on the same side. Which lesion is most likely?
why: Cholesteatoma causes conductive loss with foul discharge, not corneal reflex loss
Correct — a CPA vestibular schwannoma causes progressive unilateral SNHL and, as it enlarges, compresses CN V causing absent corneal reflex
Meniere's causes episodic vertigo with fluctuating SNHL, no CN V involvement
Otosclerosis is a conductive loss with a normal tympanic membrane, unrelated to CN V
exp: A vestibular schwannoma arises from the CN VIII sheath in the cerebellopontine angle; progressive unilateral SNHL with tinnitus plus an absent corneal reflex is the classic presentation — bilateral tumours suggest NF2, and gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the investigation of choice.

subject: ENT
q: What is the most common site of epistaxis, especially in children?
why: Wrong - Woodruff's plexus is a posterior source, more implicated in adults with hypertension/atherosclerosis
Wrong - sphenopalatine artery bleeds are posterior and less common overall
Wrong - anterior ethmoidal bleeds occur but are far less frequent than Little's area
Correct - anterior septal Little's area is the classic, most common site
exp: Little's area, an anastomotic vascular plexus on the anteroinferior nasal septum, accounts for over 90% of epistaxis episodes, particularly in children, because it is superficial and exposed to trauma, drying, and digital picking.

subject: ENT
q: As per the Paradise criteria, recurrent tonsillitis in a child is considered an indication for tonsillectomy if there have been how many documented episodes in the preceding 1 year?
why: Correct - 7 or more episodes in a single year meets the threshold
Wrong - this threshold only qualifies when sustained over 3 consecutive years, not one year
Wrong - this threshold only qualifies when sustained over 2 consecutive years, not one year
Wrong - no such single-year threshold exists in the criteria
exp: The Paradise criteria for tonsillectomy in recurrent tonsillitis require 7 or more episodes in 1 year, OR 5 or more episodes per year for 2 consecutive years, OR 3 or more episodes per year for 3 consecutive years, each episode well-documented with fever, exudate, adenopathy, or positive strep culture.

subject: ENT
q: In a patient with left-sided conductive hearing loss, which combination of Rinne and Weber test findings is expected?
opts: Rinne positive left, Weber lateralizes to right
Rinne negative left, Weber lateralizes to left
Rinne negative left, Weber lateralizes to right
why: Wrong - a positive Rinne implies a normal air-bone relationship, inconsistent with conductive loss
Correct - negative Rinne and Weber lateralizing to the same affected ear is classic for conductive loss
Wrong - Weber lateralizing away from the affected ear suggests sensorineural, not conductive, loss
Wrong - this pattern implies normal hearing bilaterally
exp: In conductive hearing loss, bone conduction exceeds air conduction on the affected side, giving a negative (abnormal) Rinne test, and the Weber test lateralizes toward the affected ear because bone-conducted sound is perceived better there without ambient air-conduction competition.

subject: ENT
q: What is the most common cause of bilateral vocal cord palsy leading to acute stridor in adults?
opts: Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury following thyroid surgery
why: Wrong - idiopathic causes are more typical of unilateral, not bilateral, palsy
Wrong - viral laryngitis causes inflammation, not nerve palsy
Correct - post-thyroidectomy nerve injury is the classic and most common cause of bilateral palsy
Wrong - malignancy is a less common cause of bilateral compared to unilateral palsy
exp: Iatrogenic injury to both recurrent laryngeal nerves during thyroidectomy is the leading cause of bilateral vocal cord palsy; because both cords lie near the midline, it commonly presents as acute stridor and airway obstruction requiring urgent tracheostomy or cord lateralization.

subject: ENT
q: What is the gold-standard investigation for diagnosing obstructive sleep apnea in an adult?
why: Wrong - Epworth score screens for daytime sleepiness but cannot diagnose or grade OSA
Wrong - lateral neck X-ray has a limited, non-diagnostic role
Wrong - nasopharyngolaryngoscopy helps localize obstruction but does not quantify apnea severity
Correct - polysomnography is the diagnostic gold standard
exp: Polysomnography objectively measures the apnea-hypopnea index, oxygen desaturation, and sleep architecture, and remains the gold-standard confirmatory test for OSA even though clinical scales and endoscopy help identify candidates and localize the site of obstruction.

subject: ENT
q: In chronic suppurative otitis media with cholesteatoma, facial nerve palsy most commonly results from erosion of which part of the fallopian (facial) canal?
why: Correct - the tympanic segment is the classic site of dehiscence and erosion
Wrong - labyrinthine segment involvement is less common and associated with other pathology
Wrong - mastoid segment erosion occurs but is less frequent than tympanic
Wrong - meatal segment is not a standard site eroded by middle ear disease
exp: The tympanic segment of the facial nerve canal is naturally the thinnest and most frequently dehiscent even in normal ears, making it the site most vulnerable to erosion by cholesteatoma or granulation tissue in chronic suppurative otitis media, leading to facial nerve palsy.

subject: ENT
q: A 22-year-old man presents with fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and no cough. His Centor score, used to predict likelihood of streptococcal pharyngitis, is:
why: Would apply if only one criterion were met, not all four described here
Would apply if only two criteria were met, not all four described here
Correct - all four Centor criteria are present, giving a score of 4
A score of 0 means none of the criteria are present, contrary to the stem
exp: The Centor criteria award one point each for fever, tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, and absence of cough; a score of 4 suggests a roughly 50-60% probability of Group A streptococcal pharyngitis and supports empirical antibiotics or rapid antigen testing.

subject: ENT
q: A 9-year-old boy with acute sinusitis develops eyelid edema, proptosis, restricted eye movements, and mild diplopia, with no visual loss. Which Chandler stage best fits this presentation?
why: Preseptal cellulitis shows lid swelling only, no proptosis or EOM restriction
Correct - localized collection causing proptosis and restricted EOM is stage III
Orbital cellulitis is diffuse without a discrete abscess and usually less EOM restriction
Orbital abscess is more advanced, often with visual loss/complete ophthalmoplegia
exp: Chandler staging of orbital complications of sinusitis: I preseptal cellulitis, II orbital cellulitis, III subperiosteal abscess (proptosis + restricted EOM), IV orbital abscess, V cavernous sinus thrombosis.

subject: ENT
q: A 6-year-old presents with inattentiveness at school and mild hearing loss, and otoscopy shows a dull, retracted tympanic membrane with an air-fluid level, without pain or fever. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Correct - painless conductive hearing loss with retracted, dull TM and air-fluid level
Acute suppurative OM presents with pain, fever, and a bulging (not retracted) TM
Cholesteatoma shows an attic retraction pocket or pearly white mass, not simple effusion
Otosclerosis is a stapes fixation disorder without effusion on otoscopy
exp: Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) is common in children, often following incomplete resolution of acute otitis media or adenoid-related eustachian tube dysfunction, and can present as school/behavioral difficulty if missed.

subject: ENT
q: A patient with chronic ear discharge undergoes otoscopy showing a perforation involving the pars tensa but not reaching the annulus, with an intact rim of tympanic membrane all around. What type of perforation and disease is this most consistent with?
opts: Marginal perforation - suggestive of cholesteatoma (unsafe CSOM)
Central perforation - suggestive of tubotympanic (safe) CSOM
why: Marginal perforation reaches the annulus, unlike the finding described
Attic perforation is in the pars flaccida (Shrapnell's membrane), not pars tensa as here
Correct - an intact rim not reaching the annulus defines a central perforation
Total/subtotal perforation involves the whole TM, not this bounded finding
exp: A central perforation, with an intact TM rim all around, is characteristic of tubotympanic (safe) type CSOM, generally without cholesteatoma; marginal or attic perforations suggest atticoantral (unsafe) CSOM.

subject: ENT
q: A farmer from rural Tamil Nadu with a history of bathing in stagnant ponds presents with unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Examination reveals a friable, strawberry-like, red polypoidal mass in the nasal cavity with tiny white dots visible on its surface. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: JNA occurs almost exclusively in adolescent males as a firm, vascular nasopharyngeal mass, not a friable strawberry lesion with white dots
Antrochoanal polyp is smooth and greyish, arising from the maxillary sinus, not friable/strawberry-coloured
Correct
Inverted papilloma is a greyish papillary mass without the classic white-dot sporangia
exp: Rhinosporidiosis, caused by Rhinosporidium seeberi and endemic in India (especially Tamil Nadu, with stagnant-water exposure), classically presents as a friable, vascular, strawberry-like polyp with pathognomonic white-dot sporangia; treatment is wide excision with cauterisation of the base given high recurrence, as there is no reliably effective antifungal therapy.

subject: ENT
q: A 16-year-old boy has a unilateral nasal polyp arising from the maxillary sinus that extends posteriorly through the ostium into the nasopharynx. What is this lesion called?
why: Ethmoidal polyps are typically bilateral and multiple, linked to allergic rhinitis
Correct — antrochoanal (Killian's) polyp arises from the maxillary sinus and extends into the choana
Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a vascular tumour presenting with epistaxis, not a polyp from the maxillary sinus
Inverted papilloma is a locally aggressive tumour with malignant potential, histologically distinct
exp: Antrochoanal (Killian's) polyp arises from the maxillary sinus mucosa, prolapses through the natural or accessory ostium, and extends into the nasal cavity and choana/nasopharynx; unlike allergic ethmoidal polyps, it is typically unilateral and single, and treated surgically with removal of the antral component.

subject: ENT
q: A 65-year-old woman reports brief episodes of spinning vertigo lasting seconds, triggered by turning over in bed or looking up, with no hearing loss or tinnitus. Which test is most useful to confirm the diagnosis?
why: Audiometry is irrelevant since hearing is normal and vertigo is positional
Correct - reproduces symptoms with characteristic torsional-upbeat nystagmus
Caloric testing evaluates vestibular function more generally, not the bedside test of choice here
MRI is reserved for atypical features suggesting a central cause
exp: Brief positional vertigo without auditory symptoms, provoked by head position change, is classic for BPPV; the Dix-Hallpike maneuver is the bedside diagnostic test of choice, reproducing symptoms with transient torsional-upbeat nystagmus (usually posterior canal), and the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver is the treatment.

subject: ENT
q: An 8-year-old boy has bilateral nasal polyps, recurrent sinusitis, chronic productive cough, and poor weight gain despite a good appetite. Which investigation should be prioritized given this combination of findings?
why: Endoscopy confirms polyps but doesn't explain the systemic picture
Allergic rhinitis and adult eosinophilic nasal polyposis are also typically bilateral, so allergy testing does not discriminate here and does not explain the cough or failure to thrive
Correct - bilateral nasal polyps with respiratory infections and failure to thrive should prompt CF screening
CT aids surgical planning but doesn't address the underlying systemic diagnosis
exp: Nasal polyps are rare before age 10, so bilateral polyps in a child should prompt exclusion of cystic fibrosis (up to ~40% of children with CF develop polyposis), and less commonly primary ciliary dyskinesia. With chronic productive cough and failure to thrive despite good appetite (pancreatic exocrine insufficiency), sweat chloride testing is the confirmatory test.

subject: ENT
q: A 40-year-old with a recent lower molar dental infection presents with rapidly progressive bilateral submandibular swelling, tongue elevation, drooling, and stridor, consistent with Ludwig's angina. The most appropriate immediate step is:
opts: IV antibiotics and observe in the ward
Awake fibreoptic intubation (or tracheostomy under local anaesthesia) to secure the airway
Contrast CT neck to define the extent of the collection
Immediate incision and drainage under general anaesthesia
why: Antibiotics are essential but do not protect an airway already threatened by tongue elevation
Correct — awake airway securing is the priority before the swelling progresses to complete obstruction
Imaging delays definitive airway control and moves an unstable patient out of a monitored area
GA induction with muscle relaxation risks a cannot-intubate-cannot-ventilate scenario; drainage follows once the airway is secured
exp: Ludwig's angina is a rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, most commonly odontogenic; it causes tongue elevation and posterior displacement that can obstruct the airway. Because inducing general anaesthesia risks losing the airway entirely, awake fibreoptic intubation or tracheostomy under local anaesthesia is the recommended first step, with antibiotics and surgical decompression following once the airway is secured.

subject: ENT
q: A 45-year-old presents with sudden unilateral hearing loss developing over 24 hours, accompanied by tinnitus, with no preceding ear infection, trauma, or barotrauma; pure tone audiometry confirms a sensorineural hearing loss. The most appropriate immediate management is:
opts: Betahistine and vasodilator therapy, review in 6 weeks
MRI of the internal auditory meati before starting any treatment
why: Betahistine/vasodilators have no proven benefit in SSNHL, and a 6-week delay squanders the treatment window
MRI is mandatory to exclude vestibular schwannoma but should be arranged in parallel, not as a prerequisite to steroids
Correct — urgent steroid therapy is the recommended emergency management
Topical drops act on the external/middle ear and cannot reach the cochlea
exp: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (typically ≥30 dB loss across at least three contiguous frequencies within 72 hours) is an otologic emergency because early treatment, generally high-dose oral or intratympanic corticosteroids started as soon as possible, improves the chances of hearing recovery; MRI to exclude retrocochlear pathology is arranged in parallel, not as a delay to steroids.

subject: ENT
q: A 17-year-old presents with fever, severe sore throat, marked tonsillar exudate, and tender posterior cervical lymphadenopathy for one week. He is empirically started on amoxicillin by a general practitioner and develops a diffuse maculopapular rash over his trunk and limbs within 2 days. Abdominal examination reveals mild splenomegaly. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
why: Correct, exudative tonsillitis, posterior cervical adenopathy, splenomegaly, and amoxicillin-triggered rash
Strep pharyngitis does not typically cause splenomegaly or this rash pattern
Diphtheria causes a grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal, not this pattern
Peritonsillar abscess causes unilateral bulging and trismus, not a rash after antibiotics
exp: The amoxicillin/ampicillin-induced rash in infectious mononucleosis is a classic, near-pathognomonic clinical clue (occurring in most EBV-infected patients given aminopenicillins) and should prompt testing (heterophile/Monospot or EBV serology) rather than being mistaken for a true penicillin allergy.

subject: ENT
q: A 45-year-old presents with episodic vertigo lasting hours, fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness in one ear. What is the underlying pathology?
why: Wrong — otosclerosis causes progressive conductive hearing loss, not episodic vertigo with fluctuating SNHL.
Correct — the classic tetrad results from endolymphatic hydrops.
Wrong — cholesteatoma causes chronic otorrhea and conductive loss; labyrinth erosion produces constant, not episodic, vertigo.
Wrong — vestibular schwannoma causes progressive unilateral SNHL and imbalance, not discrete vertigo episodes.
exp: Meniere's disease presents with the classic tetrad of episodic vertigo (20 minutes to hours), fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness, caused by endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph distending the membranous labyrinth). Managed with a low-salt diet and diuretics (betahistine, thiazides); severe refractory disease may need intratympanic gentamicin or endolymphatic sac surgery.

subject: ENT
q: A 35-year-old man with longstanding bronchial asthma develops recurrent bilateral nasal polyps and an acute wheezing episode within an hour of taking ibuprofen for headache. What is this triad called?
why: Wrong — Wegener's (GPA) is a respiratory-renal vasculitis, a different entity.
Correct — Samter's triad / aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease.
Wrong — Churg-Strauss (EGPA) is asthma with eosinophilia and vasculitis, a distinct entity.
Wrong — Charcot's triad is fever, jaundice, and right-upper-quadrant pain in ascending cholangitis.
exp: Samter's triad (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease) is asthma plus nasal polyposis plus NSAID/aspirin hypersensitivity, driven by COX-1 inhibition shunting arachidonic acid toward leukotriene synthesis. Affected patients should avoid NSAIDs and be counselled toward paracetamol or leukotriene-pathway-sparing alternatives.

subject: ENT
q: A 10-year-old boy sustains blunt trauma to the nose during a fall. Two days later he has worsening bilateral nasal obstruction with a soft, fluctuant, bluish-red swelling of the nasal septum on both sides. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Urgent incision and drainage of the septal hematoma
Reassurance and cold compress; review after a week
Oral antibiotics alone with outpatient follow-up
Immediate closed reduction of nasal bone fracture
why: Correct — the hematoma must be drained urgently since the septal cartilage depends entirely on the overlying perichondrium for its blood supply.
Delay risks avascular necrosis of the septal cartilage and subsequent saddle-nose deformity or abscess formation.
Antibiotics alone do not relieve the pressure separating the cartilage from its blood supply; drainage is still required.
Reduction of a nasal bone fracture addresses a separate injury and does not treat the more urgent septal hematoma.
exp: A bilateral, boggy, bluish-red septal swelling after nasal trauma is a septal hematoma, an ENT emergency. Because the septal cartilage receives its entire blood supply from the overlying perichondrium, an undrained hematoma causes avascular necrosis within days, leading to saddle-nose deformity or septal abscess — urgent incision and drainage (with anterior nasal packing) prevents this.

subject: ENT
q: A 45-year-old man from Northeast India presents with unilateral nasal obstruction, blood-stained nasal discharge, conductive hearing loss from serous otitis media, and a firm, non-tender cervical lymph node. Nasopharyngoscopy shows a mass arising from the fossa of Rosenmuller, and biopsy confirms non-keratinizing carcinoma. Which agent is most strongly associated with this malignancy?
why: HPV 16/18 drives cervical and oropharyngeal (tonsil/base of tongue) cancers, not the non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal type
H. pylori is linked to gastric carcinoma and MALT lymphoma, not nasopharyngeal carcinoma
Correct — EBV is the classic association, especially in endemic non-keratinizing nasopharyngeal carcinoma
HTLV-1 causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma, unrelated to nasopharyngeal carcinoma
exp: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma, especially the non-keratinizing and undifferentiated WHO subtypes seen in Southern China and parts of Northeast India, is strongly linked to EBV. Unilateral serous otitis media plus a neck node in a middle-aged patient is the classic exam triad and should trigger nasopharyngoscopy rather than a trial of ear drops.

subject: ENT
q: A 5-year-old boy has loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses during sleep, and grade 3 tonsillar hypertrophy on examination, with daytime irritability and poor school performance. What is the most appropriate definitive management?
opts: Watchful waiting with reassessment in 6 months
why: Intranasal steroids may help mild adenoidal hypertrophy but are not definitive for significant OSA with grade 3 tonsils
Antibiotics treat acute bacterial infection, not chronic hypertrophy causing OSA
Watchful waiting risks ongoing hypoxia and cardiopulmonary/cognitive sequelae, inappropriate given the symptom burden
Correct — adenotonsillectomy is first-line definitive management
exp: Adenotonsillar hypertrophy is the commonest cause of obstructive sleep apnea in children; adenotonsillectomy is first-line definitive treatment once significant OSA with marked tonsillar/adenoidal enlargement is identified, since it relieves obstruction and reverses growth, behavioural, and cardiopulmonary sequelae if left untreated.

subject: ENT
q: A term neonate has episodes of cyanosis that worsen during feeding and improve with crying. A soft catheter cannot be passed through either nostril into the nasopharynx. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Laryngomalacia causes inspiratory stridor worsened by feeding or agitation but does not prevent catheter passage through the nose
Tracheoesophageal fistula presents with choking or coughing on feeds and excess oral secretions, not failed nasal catheter passage
Pierre Robin sequence causes airway obstruction from micrognathia and glossoptosis, relieved by prone positioning, not catheter failure
Correct — neonates are obligate nasal breathers, so bilateral choanal atresia causes cyclical cyanosis relieved by crying and confirmed by failed catheter passage
exp: Neonates are obligate nasal breathers for the first few weeks of life. Bilateral choanal atresia classically presents with cyclical cyanosis, worse during quiet feeding and relieved by crying (mouth breathing), and is confirmed by failure to pass a 5-6 Fr catheter through the nose. It is associated with CHARGE syndrome and needs urgent airway support before surgical correction.

subject: ENT
q: A 6-year-old boy has loud snoring, witnessed breathing pauses during sleep, mouth breathing, and daytime irritability, with grade 3 tonsillar hypertrophy on examination. The most appropriate management is:
why: Nasal steroids may help mild adenoidal obstruction but are inadequate for marked hypertrophy with witnessed apnoea.
Reassurance risks progression to cor pulmonale, growth failure, and cognitive or behavioural sequelae - inappropriate here.
Correct - definitive treatment for significant adenotonsillar-hypertrophy-related paediatric OSA.
Polysomnography helps confirm severity or resolve an equivocal diagnosis, but is not a mandatory prerequisite before treating a classic, unambiguous clinical presentation.
exp: In a child with a clear clinical picture of obstructive sleep apnoea and marked adenotonsillar hypertrophy on examination, adenotonsillectomy is the standard first-line definitive treatment - untreated paediatric OSA risks failure to thrive, cor pulmonale, and neurocognitive or behavioural impairment, so timely surgical referral matters more than deferring for a confirmatory sleep study in classic cases. When a sleep study is required before surgery differs between guideline bodies.

subject: ENT
q: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes presents in diabetic ketoacidosis with periorbital swelling, proptosis, and a black necrotic eschar over the nasal turbinate on examination. Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Urgent surgical debridement plus intravenous amphotericin B for acute invasive fungal (mucormycosis) sinusitis
Oral itraconazole and outpatient follow-up for allergic fungal sinusitis
Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics alone for bacterial orbital cellulitis
High-dose oral corticosteroids for suspected granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's)
why: Correct - mucormycosis needs emergent debridement and IV amphotericin B; delay is fatal.
Allergic fungal sinusitis occurs in atopic, immunocompetent patients with nasal polyps, not black eschar with DKA.
Antibiotics alone will not clear fungal tissue invasion; debridement is essential.
GPA causes saddle-nose deformity/vasculitis, not an eschar in a DKA patient, and steroids would worsen a fungal infection.
exp: Black necrotic eschar over the nasal turbinate/palate in a patient with DKA or other immunocompromise is acute invasive rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis until proven otherwise - Rhizopus is the commonest agent. Management is emergency surgical debridement plus IV liposomal amphotericin B; steroids and delay are lethal.

subject: ENT
q: Zenker's diverticulum characteristically herniates through a triangular area of weakness in the posterior pharyngeal wall known as?
why: Killian-Jamieson area is a separate, more lateral weak spot below the cricopharyngeus that gives rise to a different (Killian-Jamieson) diverticulum
Passavant's ridge is a muscular bulge from superior constrictor contraction during swallowing and speech, unrelated to diverticula
Correct — Killian's dehiscence, between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus fibres of the inferior constrictor, is the classic pulsion site for Zenker's diverticulum
Laimer's triangle is a weak area below the cricopharyngeus, a much less common site for diverticula
exp: Zenker's (pharyngoesophageal) diverticulum is a pulsion diverticulum through Killian's dehiscence, the natural weak point between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor. Classic triad: dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis.

subject: ENT
q: A 2-year-old presents with fever, refusal to feed, drooling, and the neck held in extension. Image described: lateral neck X-ray showing marked widening of the prevertebral soft-tissue shadow anterior to the cervical vertebrae. Which diagnosis fits, and what is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Peritonsillar abscess - needle aspiration at the bedside
Acute laryngotracheobronchitis - humidified oxygen and steroids
Retropharyngeal abscess - contrast CT neck and surgical drainage
exp: Retropharyngeal abscess arises from suppuration of retropharyngeal lymph nodes and is classically seen in children under 4 years, presenting with fever, drooling, neck stiffness/extension, and torticollis. A lateral neck X-ray showing a widened prevertebral space (>7 mm at C2 or >14 mm at C6 in a child) is suggestive, but contrast CT confirms the diagnosis and extent before urgent surgical drainage plus IV antibiotics - it is an airway emergency distinct from peritonsillar abscess, which is intraoral with trismus and uvular deviation.

subject: ENT
q: A 3-year-old child with a 5-day history of fever and ear discharge now presents with a tender, fluctuant postauricular swelling that pushes the pinna forward and downward, along with worsening fever and lethargy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Furunculosis of the external auditory canal
why: Wrong — a canal furuncle is tender on tragal pressure and lies in the canal, not behind the ear
Wrong — Ramsay Hunt syndrome gives facial palsy with vesicles on the pinna
Wrong — Bezold's abscess tracks through the mastoid tip into the neck along sternocleidomastoid
Correct — a subperiosteal abscess from coalescent mastoiditis pushes the pinna forward and downward
exp: Acute coalescent mastoiditis follows inadequately treated acute otitis media and classically produces a postauricular subperiosteal abscess that pushes the pinna forward and downward, distinct from a canal furuncle and from Bezold's abscess (pus tracking through the mastoid tip into the neck along sternocleidomastoid). Workup needs CT temporal bone; management is IV antibiotics plus or minus cortical mastoidectomy.

subject: ENT
q: A 6-year-old boy has mouth breathing, hyponasal (stuffy) voice, and snoring for 6 months, with adenoid facies (long face, open mouth, prominent incisors) on examination. Which investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis before planning adenoidectomy?
opts: Lateral soft-tissue neck radiograph with adenoid-nasopharyngeal (AN) ratio
Flexible nasopharyngoscopy under general anaesthesia only
why: Wrong — CT sinuses adds radiation and is reserved for atypical or complicated cases
Correct — a lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray with the adenoid-nasopharyngeal ratio (Fujioka) is the standard test before adenoidectomy
Wrong — polysomnography is added only when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected
Wrong — flexible nasopharyngoscopy is usually done awake in clinic; GA is not needed just to confirm adenoid size
exp: Adenoid hypertrophy in children classically presents with mouth breathing, hyponasal voice, snoring, and adenoid facies. A lateral soft-tissue neck X-ray measuring the adenoid-nasopharyngeal (AN) ratio (Fujioka's method) is the standard bedside screening investigation before adenoidectomy; CT is reserved for atypical or complicated cases, and polysomnography is added only when obstructive sleep apnoea is suspected, not as the primary diagnostic test.

subject: ENT
q: A 28-year-old woman presents with gradually progressive bilateral hearing loss that she reports improves in noisy environments (paracusis Willisii), a normal-appearing tympanic membrane, and a family history of similar hearing loss. Image described: pure tone audiogram showing a conductive hearing loss with an air-bone gap and a dip in the bone-conduction curve at 2000 Hz. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Wrong — CSOM gives a perforated or abnormal drum, often with discharge
Correct — bilateral conductive loss with a normal drum, paracusis Willisii, family history and Carhart's notch is otosclerosis
Wrong — Meniere disease gives fluctuating sensorineural loss with vertigo and tinnitus
Wrong — presbycusis is age-related high-frequency sensorineural loss in the elderly
exp: Otosclerosis is bilateral, autosomal-dominant conductive hearing loss in young adults (more common in women, worsened by pregnancy) with a normal tympanic membrane, paracusis Willisii, and the classic audiometric Carhart's notch -- a dip in the bone-conduction curve at 2000 Hz caused by fixation of the stapes footplate, not true sensorineural loss.

subject: ENT
q: Which biochemical marker is most specific for confirming that clear nasal discharge following head trauma is cerebrospinal fluid?
why: Correct: beta-2 transferrin is found almost only in CSF, perilymph and aqueous humour
Glucose strips give false positives from glucose in blood and nasal secretions
The halo sign is only a bedside clue and is unreliable with blood-stained fluid
Beta-trace protein is useful but less specific, and is altered in renal failure and meningitis
exp: Beta-2 transferrin (tau protein) is found almost exclusively in CSF, perilymph, and aqueous humour, making it the most specific biochemical test to confirm CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea. The bedside glucose oxidase strip and the halo/ring sign on filter paper are less specific and can give false positives, especially with blood-tinged secretions.

subject: ENT
q: A 22-year-old man with sore throat for 5 days develops trismus, a muffled 'hot potato' voice, and uvular deviation to the left. What is the most likely diagnosis and its definitive treatment?
opts: Peritonsillar abscess; incision and drainage (or needle aspiration)
why: Correct: trismus, hot potato voice and contralateral uvular deviation mean quinsy; drainage plus antibiotics is definitive
Retropharyngeal abscess bulges the posterior pharyngeal wall without uvular deviation, and an abscess needs drainage
Ludwig angina is a floor-of-mouth infection that lifts the tongue; it does not deviate the uvula
Epiglottitis causes stridor and drooling without trismus or uvular deviation
exp: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) classically presents with trismus, muffled 'hot potato' voice, drooling, and contralateral uvular deviation due to a collection deep to the tonsillar capsule; treatment is drainage (aspiration or incision) plus antibiotics covering Group A Streptococcus and oral anaerobes.

subject: ENT
q: A 14-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of profuse epistaxis and progressive nasal obstruction. Image described: nasal endoscopy showing a firm, reddish-pink mass filling the nasopharynx with a smooth surface and prominent vessels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why: Antrochoanal polyp arises from the maxillary sinus and is pale and avascular, without profuse epistaxis
Correct: a vascular nasopharyngeal mass with recurrent epistaxis in an adolescent boy is JNA
Rhinosporidiosis gives a friable strawberry-like polyp in the nasal cavity, not a firm vascular nasopharyngeal mass
Nasopharyngeal carcinoma occurs in older patients and presents with neck nodes and ear symptoms
exp: Juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma is a benign but locally aggressive, highly vascular tumour arising near the sphenopalatine foramen, classically in adolescent males, presenting with recurrent severe epistaxis and nasal obstruction; contrast CT/MRI showing anterior bowing of the posterior maxillary sinus wall (Holman-Miller sign) clinches the diagnosis, and biopsy is avoided because of catastrophic bleeding risk.

subject: ENT
q: A 14-year-old has years of scanty, foul-smelling ear discharge with progressive hearing loss. Otoscopy shows a perforation in the pars flaccida with whitish debris. Most likely diagnosis?
why: Tubotympanic (safe) CSOM has a central perforation with profuse mucoid, non-foul discharge
Acute otitis media is a short illness with a bulging drum, not years of discharge
Otitis externa affects the canal skin and does not perforate the drum
Correct: attic perforation, scanty foul discharge and white keratin debris are cholesteatoma
exp: An attic (pars flaccida) perforation with scanty foul discharge is unsafe atticoantral disease - cholesteatoma. It is called unsafe because it erodes bone and causes facial palsy, labyrinthine fistula and intracranial sepsis, so it needs surgery rather than medical treatment.
